title: Empyema
subject: Medicine
summary: Empyema is pus in the pleural space, usually following pneumonia or TB. Diagnosis relies on pleural fluid analysis and imaging, and early drainage is vital to prevent mortality.

sections.p: Empyema is an infected pleural effusion where the fluid is purulent and the pleural space is colonised by bacteria.
b: Pleural fluid pH <7.2, glucose <40 mg/dL, LDH >1000 IU/L, or positive Gram stain/culture confirms infection.
Chest X‑ray shows a homogeneous opacity; ultrasound or CT identifies loculations.

sections.p: Three stages guide management: exudative (stage I), fibrinopurulent (stage II), and organized (stage III).
b: Stage I: free‑flowing fluid, pH >7.2, minimal loculation – may respond to antibiotics alone.
Stage II: fibrin strands, pH <7.2, loculated – requires chest tube drainage with fibrinolytics.
Stage III: thick peel, trapped lung – surgical decortication is often needed.

sections.p: In low‑resource settings the hierarchy of causes reflects local infection patterns.
b: Bacterial pneumonia (Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Klebsiella) – most common.
Tuberculous pleuritis – lymphocytic, high ADA, common in HIV patients.
Parapneumonic effusion after untreated malaria‑related pneumonia.
Post‑traumatic or post‑surgical pleural contamination.
Rare: fungal infection, empyema secondary to chest wall osteomyelitis.

sections.p: Patients develop pleuritic chest pain, fever, dyspnoea, and a dullness to percussion over the affected hemithorax.
b: Fever >38 °C, night sweats, weight loss (TB).
Reduced breath sounds, egophony, and pleural rub early; later absent breath sounds over fluid.
Tachypnoea and hypoxia if large or bilateral.

t.b: Is the fluid free‑flowing or loculated? → Guides chest‑tube placement; if unavailable, use bedside percussion and auscultation.

t.a: Pleural fluid analysis (pH, glucose, LDH, Gram stain, culture)
t.b: Does the effusion meet empyema criteria? → pH <7.2, glucose <40 mg/dL, LDH >1000 IU/L confirm infection; if lab unavailable, rely on clinical picture and imaging.
Is there a pleural opacity with meniscus sign? → Confirms effusion; may miss loculations.
Are there thickened pleura or lung entrapment? → Determines stage III need for surgery.
Is ADA >40 U/L with lymphocyte predominance? → Suggests tuberculous empyema; start anti‑TB therapy.

sections.p: Delayed drainage can lead to life‑threatening sequelae.
b: Septic shock, respiratory failure, or multi‑organ failure.
Bronchopleural fistula causing persistent air leak.
Trapped lung with chronic dyspnoea.
Spread to mediastinum or pericardium.

sections.p: Treat the infection, evacuate pus, and prevent recurrence.
b: Empiric IV antibiotics covering Gram‑positive, Gram‑negative, and anaerobes (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole) – adjust after culture.
Chest tube drainage; add intrapleural fibrinolytic (e.g., streptokinase) for stage II loculations.
Surgical decortication for stage III or failed drainage.
If TB confirmed, start standard 6‑month anti‑TB regimen; avoid steroids unless massive inflammation.
Supportive care: oxygen, analgesia, fluid balance, and monitor renal function.

sections.p: After drainage, ensure resolution and address underlying risk factors.
b: Repeat chest X‑ray 1‑2 weeks post‑drainage to confirm lung re‑expansion.
Vaccinate against pneumococcus and influenza.
Screen HIV patients for TB and provide prophylaxis.
Educate on early presentation for pneumonia symptoms.

sections.p: Conditions that produce pleural fluid but lack pus.
b: Parapneumonic effusion – sterile, pH >7.2, resolves with antibiotics alone.
Tuberculous pleuritis – lymphocyte‑rich, ADA high, pH often >7.2.
Hemothorax – bloody fluid, trauma history, coagulation studies abnormal.

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely reassuring.
b: Pleural fluid pH may be normal if sample exposed to air; repeat measurement promptly.
Gram stain can be negative in TB; rely on ADA and culture.
Ultrasound may miss small loculations; consider CT if clinical picture worsens.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly worsening dyspnoea, hypotension, or altered mental status – possible septic shock.
New onset chest pain with tachycardia after chest‑tube placement – suspect tension pneumothorax.

faq.q: Why is pleural fluid pH important?
faq.a: A pH <7.2 indicates bacterial metabolism and predicts failure of antibiotics alone, prompting drainage.
Early‑stage empyema often resolves with antibiotics and chest‑tube drainage; stage III usually needs decortication.

faq.q: What is the role of intrapleural fibrinolytics?
faq.a: They break fibrin septa in stage II, converting loculated pus into a free‑flowing collection for drainage.

exam: A patient with pneumonia develops a pleural effusion; pleural fluid pH is 7.1. What is the next step — immediate chest‑tube drainage because low pH defines empyema.
How does tuberculous empyema differ from bacterial empyema in fluid analysis — lymphocyte predominance and ADA >40 U/L versus neutrophils and low pH.
Why is intrapleural streptokinase preferred over systemic fibrinolysis in stage II empyema — it acts locally, avoids systemic bleeding risk.
A HIV‑positive patient presents with weight loss and pleural effusion; ADA is 80 U/L. What diagnosis is most likely — tuberculous empyema, start anti‑TB therapy.
What complication should you monitor for after chest‑tube insertion for empyema — bronchopleural fistula causing persistent air leak.

In a resource‑limited hospital without CT, how would you decide between chest‑tube drainage and surgical referral — use ultrasound for loculation and pleural peel thickness; if thick peel >1 cm, refer for surgery.
Explain why routine use of steroids is avoided in bacterial empyema — they suppress immune response and may worsen infection.
What are the key elements of follow‑up after empyema resolution — repeat imaging, ensure lung re‑expansion, vaccinate, and treat underlying risk factors.
